title: Adverse Possession 12-Year Rule in Bangladesh
metaDescription: Protect ancestral or NRB land from 12-year adverse possession claims under the Limitation Act 1908. Learn legal defences and eviction remedies in Bangladesh.
heroIntro: Under Articles 142 and 144 and Section 28 of the Limitation Act, 1908, a person in continuous, open, and hostile possession of private land for 12 years without the owner's permission can extinguish the recorded owner's title. However, NRB and resident owners can defeat adverse possession claims by proving permissive occupancy, filing a Section 8 recovery suit, or prosecuting unlawful grabbing under the Bhumi Oporadh Protirodh o Protikar Ain, 2023.

quickAnswer.heading: At a Glance: 12-Year Adverse Possession Law
points: Governing Statutes: Limitation Act, 1908 (Sections 28, Articles 142, 144 & 149) and Specific Relief Act, 1877 (Sections 8 & 9).
Limitation Period: 12 years for private land; 60 years for government/khas land under Article 149.
Criminal Remedy: Summary eviction and up to 7 years imprisonment under the Bhumi Oporadh Protirodh o Protikar Ain, 2023.
Indicative Court Fee: Ad valorem court fee under Section 7(v) of the Court-Fees Act, 1870 (official schedule governs).

sections.h2: How the 12-Year Adverse Possession Rule Works in Bangladesh
sections.content:
Section 28 of the Limitation Act, 1908 provides that at the determination of the period limited to any person for instituting a suit for possession of any property, their right to such property is extinguished. Combined with Articles 142 and 144 of the First Schedule to the Limitation Act, 1908, this creates a strict 12-year limitation window from the date of dispossession or the date possession becomes adverse.

For Non-Resident Bangladeshis (NRBs) living in the UK, USA, Canada, or the Middle East, long absences often invite encroachers, neighbours, or distant relatives to occupy vacant plots or agricultural parcels. Crucially, the 12-year clock does not start merely because the owner lives abroad; it starts only when the occupant asserts an open, hostile title adverse to the true owner. Meanwhile, government khas land carries a 60-year limitation under Article 149.

To verify whether your title remains intact on official rolls before filing suit, review our guide on how to check land ownership, khatian, and mutation online or consult a dedicated land lawyer in Bangladesh.

sections.h2: Essential Legal Elements a Claimant Must Prove
sections.content:
Bangladeshi civil courts and the Appellate Division apply the classical doctrine of nec vi, nec clam, nec precario—meaning possession must be peaceful, open, and without permission—before title can pass by prescription. The burden of proof rests heavily on the person claiming adverse possession, not on the recorded owner holding a registered Saf Kabala deed.

Legal ElementStatutory / Judicial RequirementWhat Defeats the Claim
Actual & Exclusive ControlContinuous physical occupation (fencing, cultivation, structure) for 12 uninterrupted years.Seasonal or sporadic trespass, or shared possession with the owner.
Hostile Intent (Animus Possidendi)Open denial of the recorded owner's title under Article 144, Limitation Act 1908.Rent receipts, caretaking letters, or barga (sharecropping) agreements.
Open & Notorious UseVisible occupation that a diligent owner could discover.Secret encroachment or shifting boundary pegs without notice.
Uninterrupted 12 YearsNo break in possession and no acknowledgment of owner's title under Section 19.Any written acknowledgment, mediation agreement, or prior eviction suit.

If an encroacher forged mutation or khatian entries to fake hostility, you can seek cancellation under land possession recovery law in Bangladesh and review NRB land protection checklists.

sections.h2: Why Permissive Caretakers and Relatives Cannot Claim Title
sections.content:
Under settled principles of the Limitation Act, 1908 and Evidence Act, 1872 (Section 116), permissive possession—such as a relative, caretaker, tenant, or co-sharer looking after NRB property—never ripens into adverse possession regardless of how many decades pass. A licensee or tenant is legally estopped from denying the landlord's or owner's title during the continuance of the permission.

In family properties, possession by one co-sharer is presumed in law to be possession on behalf of all co-sharers unless an explicit ouster is proved—meaning a clear, communicated denial of the other co-sharers' rights followed by 12 years of exclusive holding. NRB heirs facing relatives refusing to vacate ancestral homesteads can enforce their shares through a family property partition suit and verify Muslim inheritance distribution rules.

Always execute a written caretaker licence or registered lease rather than informal verbal arrangements, and pay annual land development tax (Khajna) in the owner's own name to create an unbroken paper trail of possession.

sections.h2: Step-by-Step Legal Remedies for NRB and Resident Owners
sections.content:
If someone has occupied your land or is approaching the 12-year mark, act immediately through civil or statutory criminal forums to stop the limitation clock.

  1. Serve a Formal Legal Notice: Issue an advocate's notice revoking any implied permission and demanding vacant possession within 15 to 30 days, establishing the exact date possession became unlawful.
  2. File Summary Recovery Within 6 Months (Section 9, Specific Relief Act 1877): If you were dispossessed forcibly without due process within the last 6 months, file a Section 9 suit—no title proof is required, only prior possession.
  3. File Title & Possession Suit (Section 8, Specific Relief Act 1877): If dispossession occurred between 6 months and 12 years ago, file a regular civil suit for declaration of title and recovery of khas possession in the Assistant Judge or Joint District Judge Court.
  4. Invoke Bhumi Oporadh Protirodh o Protikar Ain, 2023: Under Sections 4, 7, and 8 of the 2023 Act, file a complaint before the Executive Magistrate or District Commissioner for summary restoration of unlawfully grabbed land.
  5. Execute Through Embassy Power of Attorney: NRBs unable to travel can authorise a relative or Advocate Md. Shah Alam via an Embassy-attested Power of Attorney from abroad.

For urgent boundary interference, also consider criminal defence and bail options if counter-cases are filed during land disputes.

sections.h2: Documents Checklist to Defeat Adverse Possession
sections.content:
Compile these original and certified records to prove continuous ownership, tax payment, and permissive origin before the civil court:

  • Original registered Saf Kabala, Heba, or partition deed (or certified copy from the Sub-Registry Office).
  • Complete chain of Khatian records (CS, SA, RS, BS/City Jarip) and updated Mutation Khatian (Namjari).
  • Up-to-date Land Development Tax (Khajna/Dakhila) receipts paid in the owner's name.
  • Written caretaker agreement, rent receipts, electricity/gas bills, or bank remittance slips showing maintenance payments.
  • Embassy-attested Power of Attorney (if the owner is an NRB prosecuting the suit from abroad) and online land record extracts.

faqs.question: Can a caretaker or tenant claim adverse possession in Bangladesh after 12 years?
faqs.answer: No. Under the Limitation Act, 1908 and Section 116 of the Evidence Act, 1872, permissive possession by a caretaker, tenant, or licensee never becomes adverse regardless of duration, unless they openly repudiate the owner's title and hold exclusively for 12 years thereafter.

faqs.question: Does living abroad as an NRB stop the 12-year limitation clock?
faqs.answer: Living abroad does not automatically pause limitation under the Limitation Act, 1908. However, the 12-year period under Article 144 runs only from the date possession turns hostile. Paying Khajna regularly and keeping written caretaker agreements prevents hostility from arising.

faqs.question: What is the difference between Section 8 and Section 9 of the Specific Relief Act?
faqs.answer: Section 9 allows summary recovery within 6 months of forcible dispossession based solely on prior possession without proving title. Section 8 applies after 6 months (within 12 years) and requires proving both ownership title and entitlement to possession.

faqs.question: Can someone claim adverse possession over government khas land?
faqs.answer: Private individuals cannot claim 12-year adverse possession over government or khas land. Under Article 149 of the Limitation Act, 1908, the limitation period against the Government is 60 years, and the Bhumi Oporadh Ain, 2023 penalises encroachment on public land.

faqs.question: How can an NRB file an eviction suit without travelling to Bangladesh?
faqs.answer: An NRB can execute a special or general Power of Attorney at the nearest Bangladesh Embassy or Consulate, get it attested by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Dhaka, and authorise a family member or advocate to file and conduct the civil suit.
